beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: There is truth out there.
beats.got: The output looks equally confident whether or not the sources back it. The poetic opening is not needed.

beats.trigger: at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect
beats.got: Per-step errors compound across a workflow. Ten steps at 85% leaves one task in five correct, which I can check myself on a calculator. It is labelled illustrative, which I respect.

beats.trigger: Round 1: 10% fabricated → 1% after fix.
beats.got: Test, fix and retest cuts the error rate by 10x each round. It starts from an assumed 10% and 90% catch rate, so I'd want the real numbers. At least the figures are stated.

beats.trigger: asking the agent "Are you sure?" returns another answer from the same source, in the same confident voice.
beats.got: Asking the AI to double-check itself is worthless. That is a useful risk to have named before I had to raise it.

beats.trigger: You don't know which detection method catches what matters on *your* output
beats.got: Test the candidate checks on your own data and don't take anyone's word for which works. This is how I would buy anything.

beats.trigger: **4. Counter-evidence search.** Look for sources that contradict each claim.
beats.got: Four checks: unsourced claims, overreach, fake citations, contradicting evidence. It is a bit jargon-heavy, but the list is clear enough.

beats.got: The agent proposes, a check or I review, and only then does it act. That is a four-eyes principle.

beats.got: A human signs off on important actions, with the check's limits in front of them. Sensible. More homework reading, though.

beats.got: Traceable to a source is not the same as true. Four short points I could repeat.

beats.got: More reading. Not doing it.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build
beats.got: Next step is 300 claims and running the check on every build. It sounds like it costs real money, and nobody says how much.

take_homes: A long AI workflow with no checks gets most results wrong even when each step is mostly right. Ten steps at 85% leaves about one in five correct.
Asking the AI 'are you sure?' proves nothing. A separate check, tested against known errors and scored, is the only thing I could defend.
A check should be saved with its known limit written down, and the AI's own report on its work is not evidence until someone re-reads the file.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run the month-end variance commentary through a source check: every number in the text compared to the ledger, with a short list of what the check cannot catch.
monday.when: Month-end close, once, on one report
monday.stop_condition: If the check misses anything a person catches in the same report, or takes more time than the commentary does, I drop it.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and the module never said what a hundred-claim run costs or where the data goes.

misconception.why: I arrived thinking AI is a licence you buy. Here you build and measure your own check from your own material and keep it as a file. That is something the organisation has to build, not just buy. It was never said outright, and the module never put a price on it, so I'm only partly moved.

one_line: Good on the idea that errors compound and that you must test the checker, but it never says what it costs, and half of it is another company's legal cases.
